title: Death of Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose
description: Figure caption, Watch: Presley Gerber seen alongside his family on the red carpetByChris Graham and Grace Eliza GoodwinOfficials are investigating the
body: Figure caption, Watch: Presley Gerber seen alongside his family on the red carpetByChris Graham and Grace Eliza GoodwinOfficials are investigating the death of Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, as a suspected overdose, Santa Monica police said on Monday. The 27-year-old model died at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records. The exact cause of death has not been determined, police said, adding there was no indication of foul play.Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US partner CBS News: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Presley Gerber became a model like his mother and sisterHe went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.In recent years, Presley Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use. In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do." And in this month's American Vogue, external, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone."I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."She added: "My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn't share anything - and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, 'I'm gonna be very human for everyone.' There's only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you're ashamed of them."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gerber (left) was a model and had spoken about his close relationship with his familyGerber had previously spoken of his close relationship with his family, including Kaia, who he appeared alongside in a campaign for Calvin Klein in 2018, and whose name he had tattooed on his arm.He told People Magazine that year: "We're a close family, especially me and my sister, so it's definitely cool. "We get to travel together half of the time, so it makes it a lot less lonely."Gerber also starred alongside his mother in Pepsi's 2018 Super Bowl commercial, 26 years after Crawford first appeared in her famous 1992 advertisement for the brand."We're a really tight family, so it was just like going to work with one of your friends. It was so fun, and easy," he told People Magazine at the time.In July, Crawford shared two childhood photographs of her son on Instagram to mark his 27th birthday."I'm so proud of the man you've become, but I'll always see you as my little boy! Love you," she wrote.If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: Death of Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose

title: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN
description: A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes agai
body: A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity.  The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people. Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law.The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean."Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video.But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law"."There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded.BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people".The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September. However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking.Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted.However, Nicolás Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year. Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election.

schema.headline: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN

title: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says
description: Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building.M
body: Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building.Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called "the most massive" attack. The region's governor said at least two people were killed and 20 injured.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region with drones and missiles, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine".Ukrainian officials meanwhile said nine people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Andrei Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured.An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Governor Andrei Vorobyev added.Videos verified by the BBC on social media show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse.Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and the oil refinery - where Ukrainian military officials said three key units had been damaged.The site supplies more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, according to the defence ministry in Kyiv, and some of its petrol, diesel and aviation fuel go to Russia's military.Ukraine's defence minister said attacking such facilities "directly undermines the enemy's ability to continue its war of aggression and supply its military formations".Sobyanin said the major attack was "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election, which was in its third day on Sunday. The vote is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and has been dismissed by critics as neither free, fair nor transparent.Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission.Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed.It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Saturday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital.In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.Russia also struck a monastery in the Kherson region with a drone on Saturday, Zelensky said, killing one member of the clergy and injuring four others.Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so.Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India.The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

schema.headline: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says

title: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex
description: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipersFigure caption, A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as pro
body: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipersFigure caption, A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in AprilByGrace Eliza GoodwinUS President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.Image source, Getty Images"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are. Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month. A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.Image caption, Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles.The Department of Defence declined to provide additional details when reached for comment.Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.

schema.headline: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex

title: Ethiopia conflict: Seven armed groups form alliance against Abiy Ahmed
description: Several of the rebel groups which have been fighting the Ethiopian authorities in different parts of the country have announced they have formed an al
body: Several of the rebel groups which have been fighting the Ethiopian authorities in different parts of the country have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa.The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival.The seven groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration.Abiy's spokesperson Billene Seyoum said the groups had already been collaborating for some time, Reuters reports.The BBC has asked the government for comment.Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country.There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions.An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement.Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states.The states are structured largely based on their dominant ethnic groups – a system of ethnic federalism that gives some autonomy to the states, but which can present social and political challenges for the country which has more than 80 ethnic groups.Some of the rebel groups in the new alliance have previously fought against each other but they say they will now work together against their common enemy.However analyst Edward Bach from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft told the AFP news agency that the groups were "unlikely to share weapons... as your ally today can be your enemy tomorrow".Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the Tigray war.It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm.Abdikadir Addaani Hirmooge, the spokesman for the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), which is part of the alliance, told the BBC that the groups in the new coalition were working to bring together communities that have been divided against one another."Our objective is for the communities to have democracy and to exercise their right to self-determination, to genuinely govern themselves," he said.He said that the government had not respected a peace deal signed in 2018 to end the conflict in the Somali region."Ethnic conflict, insecurity, and mutual oppression and pushing each other aside have not been eradicated, resulting in a need that has affected every ethnic group," he said.The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018.The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea.Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities"."Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July.The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties.The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results. The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll.

schema.headline: Ethiopia conflict: Seven armed groups form alliance against Abiy Ahmed

title: Ekurhuleni killings: Two charged with murder in South Africa over woman's body in Dawn Park
description: Two women have been charged in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg – the last of nine recent cases i
body: Two women have been charged in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg – the last of nine recent cases in that region that have reignited the debate about the levels of gender-based violence in the country.Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the two as a "breakthrough".Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice".The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.A man who was also arrested has been released without charge.Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday.Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.Addressing journalists on Monday, deputy police chief Lt Gen Tebello Mosikili said that "a team of analysts are working hard to see if there are links to all these cases" but the killing of Ntimba "appears to be an indication of a murder that stemmed from a relationship... this includes... a possible love triangle".South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. It also has a very high murder rate and though officials statistics do not identify the gender of the victims, a recent estimate from the country's Human Rights Commission indicated that, on average, six women were murdered every day between April and June this year.The recent grim discoveries have sparked a national outcry about the scale of the problem and increased the feeling of insecurity for many women.

schema.headline: Ekurhuleni killings: Two charged with murder in South Africa over woman's body in Dawn Park

title: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring
description: Image source, McQueenImage caption, Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fus
body: Image source, McQueenImage caption, Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fused severe tailoring with dark romanticismByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporter and Emma LynchPicture EditorThis London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs. The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years  of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us".Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses.Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers.Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth".Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026:Messy girl aestheticImage source, Shutterstock/Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Rejecting "quiet luxury" uniforms, Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey, and Conner Ives led London Fashion Week's embrace of the "messy girl" aesthetic by championing deliberate chaos, pairing intentionally undone tailoring and messy updos"The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season.She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year.Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion. She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy".This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives.Gardening-coreImage source, NOWFASHION via Shutterstock/Getty Images/Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Erdem, Yuhan Wang, and Bora Aksu channelled a "gardencore" vibe, trading quiet luxury for unpolished, allotment-ready chaos - pairing parkas and structured trench outerwear with kitchen-garden detailsAccording to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world.A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower. "There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats. It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu.Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show.Modern goddessImage source, Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Dujancourt's free-spirited aesthetic, organic draping, trailing ribbons, and delicately hitched slip skirtsWhilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film. Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer.Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes".Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics.Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide."Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes.OrangeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi showcased some orange Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year.Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet's matching neon outfits , externalat the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway.Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days.BalletImage source, Victor VIRGILE/Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, A school sports hall is transformed into a ballet stage for Edeline Lee's latest collection which drew inspiration from the intense discipline, repetition, and physical toll of classical danceEver the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet.After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year.Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall. "Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel."Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

schema.headline: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring

title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US
description: "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted
body: "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said during a Q&A at the Lib Dem party conference."So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."Trump had for months threatened to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.Following the announcement of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.Burnham has spoken to Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intended to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home", including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

schema.headline: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US

title: 'Far from their best' to 'a joy to watch' -  ranking Premier League teams' start to season
description: There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October.We are five matches into the league season and there is a
body: There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October.We are five matches into the league season and there is a long way to go in the campaign, but which teams have impressed so far and who have disappointed?You can have your say in the comments at the bottom of the page.Arsenal: Solid start to their title defence until they were ripped apart by Brighton having survived a penalty scare at Sunderland. 7Aston Villa: Signs they are beginning to move in the right direction after losing so many key players during the transfer window. 6Bournemouth: If games lasted 80 minutes the Cherries would be near the top of the table. Need to cut out conceding so late. 6Brentford: Demolished Spurs and Chelsea without fuss during a highly impressive unbeaten start. Can they keep it up and challenge for Europe? 8Brighton: Kings of entertainment after hitting 16 goals in five top-flight games, including three against champions Arsenal. A joy to watch. 9 Chelsea: After a strong start under Xabi Alonso, the Blues have lost two of their past three - and were picked apart by Brentford. Are they really moving in the right direction? 6Coventry City: You could hear the sighs of relief in the away end at Nottingham Forest on Saturday. Will Frank Lampard's side kick on after that win? 6Crystal Palace: Room for improvement after one win and three defeats. 5Everton: Despite a transfer window to forget, David Moyes has made the Toffees hard to beat. 6 Fulham: Decent draws against Liverpool and Manchester United but need a win. Ipswich (away) followed by Hull (home), Coventry (away) and Crystal Palace (home) offer hope when they return from the international break. 5 Hull City: To have eight points from a tough opening five fixtures is an excellent return, including beating Manchester United and drawing with Aston Villa and Chelsea. 8Ipswich Town: Defensively vulnerable but two late winners, against Sunderland and Crystal Palace, have earned them six points and shown their fighting spirit. 5Leeds United: Fifth in the league, unbeaten and with the joint-best defensive record. They showed what they are capable of with a superb 4-1 win over Newcastle. 7Liverpool: Unbeaten but have been far from their best. Three clean sheets in their past three games, but more is expected from Andoni Iraola's side. 6Manchester City: Five league games, five victories. Managed to win at Manchester United despite going down to 10 men midway through the first half. With Erling Haaland already top scorer, City fans will expect a real push to win the league. 9Manchester United: Disappointing performances to lose at Hull and draw at a Fulham side who were bottom of the league. Their only win so far came against Ipswich and they were denied a victory at Everton by a late equaliser. 4Newcastle United: A mixed bag under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They impressed in a draw against Liverpool, won comfortably at Tottenham, but were also terrible in a loss at Leeds, although they responded well to beat Hull. 6Nottingham Forest: Their best results have come away, drawing at Liverpool and winning at Aston Villa. But their home form will be a huge worry - yet to score a goal and with only one point from three matches at the City Ground. 5Sunderland: After coming seventh in 2025-26, Sunderland fans will have wanted a better start to this season. The Black Cats gave good accounts of themselves against Arsenal and Manchester City, but lost both matches. 5Tottenham Hotspur: After spending more than £300m in the summer, Spurs have been poor, failing to score in their opening four league matches. Supporters will be demanding an instant improvement after the international break. 2

schema.headline: 'Far from their best' to 'a joy to watch' -  ranking Premier League teams' start to season

title: Millions urged to evacuate as Typhoon Dujuan hits Japan
description: Figure caption, Watch: Timelapse shows typhoon barrelling towards JapanByJamie Whitehead  and Kurumi MoriTokyo correspondent Almost two million people
body: Figure caption, Watch: Timelapse shows typhoon barrelling towards JapanByJamie Whitehead  and Kurumi MoriTokyo correspondent Almost two million people are under evacuation orders in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan batters a number of the country's prefectures.The country's public broadcaster, NHK, reported that two people had died and four others were missing as a result of the typhoon. It also reported four were missing in Kanagawa prefecture.  Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life", but several weather warnings have now been downgraded.Strong winds caused power cuts for more than 50,000 people, while hundreds of flights have been cancelled and rail services have been suspended. Dujuan has had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h.Image source, EPAImage caption, Pedestrians caught in the rain at the Shibuya crossing in Tokyo The typhoon is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms.Authorities have advised the public to pay attention to weather information. Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, has hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events.Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival have been cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, has also cancelled Monday's programme.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered her condolences in a post on X to those who lost thier lives in the typhoon, before saying she would be continuing with her scheduled trip the United States as planned.  "With a sense of urgency, I instructed Chief Cabinet Secretary Takehara and Minister Hosono to respond with utmost preparedness," she wrote, before saying she had boarded a flight to the US. She will be speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, and will meet with US President Donald Trump.  Image source, ReutersImage caption, Passengers waiting for updates at Haneda AirportThe Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman who lived in the house, aged in her 60s, may have been swept away and is believed to have been buried alive. Following a search by rescue crews, she was found inside the home and pronounced dead, NHK reported. Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site.The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital before his death was confirmed, according to local reports. Police are investigating the details of the incident.Firefighters in Kanagawa prefecture said they received a call from a man who reported his house had been crushed by a landslide. Image source, EPAImage caption, A woman struggles with her umbrella outside Shinjuku stationSome research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions.As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however.Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds.And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Another woman also struggles with an umbrella in Chiba This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor.El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit.Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example.The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday. Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi and Mark Poynting, climate reporter

title: Merz vows to keep ruling coalition together for sake of Germany's 'democratic future'
description: Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-right CDU. "This elect
body: Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-right CDU. "This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he acknowledged.Merz said there had been no discussion about his own position since the results and pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings alone were behind the election defeats."I know that I as an individual played a role in these state elections," Merz said, before adding: "But the reasons for the results go far beyond just me.""We are witnessing a profound transformation of Germany's political party system, as is happening in many other countries around the world."There have been rumours Merz, who has only been in power for 16 months, could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap due to his poor approval ratings.Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave."The two elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory.In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area. Merz earlier conceded that this result was "a disaster".While the AfD won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it was far short of a majority and is unlikely to govern as other parties may refuse to work with it.Some branches of the party are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects. But its anti-immigration, Germany first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.In Berlin, the CDU's defeat means Die Linke, which won the most votes, could now take power in a coalition. Elif Eralp, who led the party to victory in the capital, promised to tackle unaffordable rent prices in remarks made after the results came out."The people of Berlin have clearly opted for a change in policy, specifically for an affordable Berlin, for policies that solve the rent crisis and put people first," she told German news outlet The Pioneer.During the election campaign, Eralp pledged to expropriate more than 200,000 housing units from private landlords. Merz has promised to pursue legislation to prevent such actions, citing the impact on foreign investment.

schema.headline: Merz vows to keep ruling coalition together for sake of Germany's 'democratic future'

title: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister says
description: Image source, Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty ImagesByEconomics editorThe UK should "team up" with a proposed economic alliance between Canada and Europe,
body: Image source, Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty ImagesByEconomics editorThe UK should "team up" with a proposed economic alliance between Canada and Europe, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said."This is all about the substance, to build an alliance of the future," he told the BBC. "The world has changed. America has changed. So we need to change."Champagne also gave a frank assessment of the Canada-US trade war after a deal collapsed last month, saying the country had "stood up for our industries, our workers, our country" by imposing tariffs.His comments come after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to an associate EU membership for Canada, an unprecedented move for the bloc.Figure caption, Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU?Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to address the EU in Strasbourg, shortly after von der Leyen's proposal was made, was "to build the alliance of the future", Champagne said.Carney, the former governor of the Bank of England, has previously talked about an alliance of "middle powers" working together on economic growth, resilience and security.Champagne told the BBC that the UK and Canada had shared values."We need to look at partnership in a different way and the great thing is that when you look at Canada - and I would say the United Kingdom - we share the same values. We are very aligned in our vision of the world. Why don't we team up?" he said."We are independent and sovereign, but we are stronger together."After his return to the White House last year, US President Donald Trump imposed sweeping global tariffs, including on long-standing trade allies such as the UK.While the UK renegotiated a trade deal with the US in June last year, the new Canada-EU alliance does raise questions for the UK's post-Brexit positioning with Europe, as well as its position with the US, after some changes of presidential rhetoric over the Falklands and Irish unity in recent weeks.Carney met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool in the middle of his trip to Brussels and Strasbourg last week, while Champagne attended a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday, alongside Chancellor John Healey.Figure caption, Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with EuropeThe developing discussions around closer ties between the EU and Canada come as Ottawa remains locked in an escalating trade war with the US, with both sides imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after talks broke down at the last moment in August.Trump has also threatened further tariffs on the EU if the associate membership plan proved "hostile" to the US, calling the idea laughable and labelling Canada a "terrible trading partner".Champagne said the trade war was not a conflict chosen by Canada."We responded because at some stage you have to say 'enough is enough'. No one can infringe on our economic sovereignty... the world took notice," he said.The minister said Canada did not seek escalation after its "measured, targeted and strategic... dollar-for-dollar, tariff-for-tariff" response and the country would "re-engage at the right time" with its southern neighbour. Affected industries would be supported "as long as it takes and whatever it takes", he added.Champagne argued that Canada's strong fiscal position helped underpin its resilience, and that the dispute with the US provided a "golden opportunity" to diversify. This is the backdrop to the promise of an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the EU, and the idea of "teaming up" with the UK too.Burnham will meet Trump for the first time this week, in New York at the UN General Assembly.Last year, after his election, Carney invited King Charles to open the Canadian Parliament in Ottawa, a move widely seen as a rebuff to Trump's repeated suggestion that Commonwealth Canada could become part of the US.The detail of the offer made by the EU to negotiate "associate membership" for Canada is yet to be formalised.Champagne said this was "a moment of great opportunities" and to strengthen the existing relationship between Canada and the EU.Carney last week pointed to Canadian membership of EU university, scientific research, AI and defence funding schemes, as well as for young Canadians and Europeans to "cross the ocean and be able to study and live".He said Canada could supply critical minerals and gas and would seek access to European advanced technologies.It is understood that both Canada and the EU see the opportunity for a process for like-minded nations which might not ever be full members, for example Australia.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister says

title: Flight disruption: Airlines criticise air traffic control over second glitch in a month
description: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.EasyJ
body: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the service, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.Nats said a "connectivity issue" at Prestwick was behind the disruption across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England - and had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick earlier this month.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said further issues today "cause even greater concern" about the UK's air traffic control.When asked by reporters whether he would look to fire the head of Nats, Burnham said "these are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated".He added that the transport secretary was taking the issues "extremely seriously" and initially it's a matter for her "to get to the bottom of... and why there has been a recurrence."The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity", although officials warned of knock-on effects.A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".More than 150 flights were cancelled at UK airports on Monday - including 140 departures and 137 arrivals, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 48 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 13 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".An independent review by the CAA into the resilience of the UK's air traffic control system is under way and the results will be published "within six months", it said.Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure". Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership.Asked on BBC Radio 4's World at One programme if Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?"Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure.Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers.British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing".A Nats spokesperson apologised, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible."What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority."They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation was "deeply frustrating" for passengers. Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot".He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their EasyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning.Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled.She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived.Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time".

schema.headline: Flight disruption: Airlines criticise air traffic control over second glitch in a month

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
description: Trump, reacting to news of the lawsuit, called the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean"
body: Trump, reacting to news of the lawsuit, called the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements. "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.He added that "almost without question" his team will file an appeal.The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.The statement from CNN, Politico and MS NOW said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting."Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."The media organisations filed the lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington, asking a judge to quickly rule Trump's ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it.On Monday morning, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties, which sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place".CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally due to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday.But on Monday morning, the five-seat CNN booth in the basement of the White House press area - typically manned throughout the day from the early hours of the morning - was empty and closed. Screens and monitors inside were turned off.Instead, a CNN crew was outside the secured area of the White House grounds, broadcasting live from a public pavement.Five TV networks, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, issued a joint statement: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government."No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."Those five networks are considered the only ones with the money and infrastructure to distribute live coverage from the White House and presidential events.For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.Several US outlets also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday.Later on Monday, Trump met with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for an hour-long discussion. Afterwards, the two held a news conference, which was covered by New York media."I told the president that we're going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in," Mamdani said.Trump continued his criticism of the media at the event, saying that journalists always say that they will boycott, but they "never boycott" him.On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel on its site called Trump TV, which began by replaying remarks from Trump during a visit to Mount Rushmore in July.Announcing his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".The US president added that there "may be others to join them".When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS Now and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

schema.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban

title: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband says he forgave her so he would not be 'eaten up inside forever'
description: The prosecution had alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months
body: The prosecution had alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.Clancy, now 36, was then left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. She attended the trial in a wheelchair.Patrick Clancy testified during the trial about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth. Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both."I didn't know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he told CBS, the BBC's US news partner. It was her mental health that led to Patrick Clancy deciding later to forgive her."I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom', and 'Baby Murderer', 'Monster'. And none of them were accurate," he said in the interview. "I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever."Asked if he felt he had failed in some way in this period leading up to the killings, he said: "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day."Living with his grief in the weeks after the tragedy became a struggle and he admitted having suicidal thoughts. "I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he said. During the seven week trial, Patrick was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.There were claims he was to blame for the murders in some way. Thrust into the limelight, tabloids snapped photos of him travelling and with his new wife Rachel Danis.The 36-year-old said the speculation was "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children. It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health".It was also "painful to see" for him personally. "And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said.The intense scrutiny prompted him to move from Duxbury to New York City in a bid to seek anonymity.Now he is starting a family with Danis and looking forward to telling his future children about their siblings. "I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids. And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister."The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband says he forgave her so he would not be 'eaten up inside forever'
